question: Inherited hyperammonemia is a result of deficiency of which enzyme of Krebs-Henseleit urea cycle?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "N-acetyl glutamate synthetase" -> "deficiency leads to decreased production of N-acetylglutamate" -> "reduced activation of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I" -> "decreased urea cycle function" -> "increased ammonia levels" -> "hyperammonemia" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Malate dehydrogenase" -> "involved in the citric acid cycle, not urea cycle" -> "deficiency does not directly lead to hyperammonemia" -> "no direct link to inherited hyperammonemia" -> 10%
CHAIN: "Isocitrate dehydrogenase" -> "part of the citric acid cycle, not urea cycle" -> "deficiency does not directly lead to hyperammonemia" -> "no direct link to inherited hyperammonemia" -> 10%
CHAIN: "Succinate dehydrogenase" -> "involved in the citric acid cycle, not urea cycle" -> "deficiency does not directly lead to hyperammonemia" -> "no direct link to inherited hyperammonemia" -> 10%
analysis: The question asks about the enzyme deficiency leading to inherited hyperammonemia in the context of the Krebs-Henseleit urea cycle. Among the options provided, N-acetyl glutamate synthetase is the only enzyme directly involved in the urea cycle. The other enzymes listed (Malate dehydrogenase, Isocitrate dehydrogenase, and Succinate dehydrogenase) are involved in the citric acid cycle, not the urea cycle. N-acetyl glutamate synthetase is crucial for the synthesis of N-acetylglutamate, an essential allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the first enzyme of the urea cycle. Deficiency in N-acetyl glutamate synthetase leads to reduced activation of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, resulting in hyperammonemia due to the inability to convert ammonia to urea efficiently.
